claim: Topographic cortical maps are essential for spatial localisation of sensory stimulation and generation of appropriate task-related motor responses.
source: Topographic cortical maps are essential for spatial localisation of sensory stimulation and generation of appropriate task-related motor responses.
evidence: This is a general statement about cortical maps supported by established scientific knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Somatosensation and nociception are finely mapped and aligned in the adult somatosensory (S1) cortex.
source: Somatosensation and nociception are finely mapped and aligned in the adult somatosensory (S1) cortex
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research in the introduction section.

claim: In infancy, when pain behaviour is disorganised and poorly directed, nociceptive maps may be less refined.
source: but in infancy, when pain behaviour is disorganised and poorly directed, nociceptive maps may be less refined.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the abstract, based on inference from observed infant pain behavior.

claim: Within S1 cortex, touch and lance of the heel elicit localised, partially overlapping increases in oxygenated haemoglobin concentration (Δ[HbO]).
source: Within S1 cortex, touch and lance of the heel elicit localised, partially overlapping increases in oxygenated haemoglobin concentration (Δ[HbO])
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fNIRS measurements presented in the study.

claim: While touch activation was restricted to the heel area, lance activation extended into cortical hand regions.
source: but while touch activation was restricted to the heel area, lance activation extended into cortical hand regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data and image reconstructions shown in the figures.

claim: The data reveals a widespread cortical nociceptive map in infant S1, consistent with their poorly directed pain behaviour.
source: The data reveals a widespread cortical nociceptive map in infant S1, consistent with their poorly directed pain behaviour.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data and its interpretation in the context of infant behavior.

claim: In adults, overlapping regions are involved in the cortical processing of noxious and innocuous mechanical stimulation.
source: In adults, overlapping regions are involved in the cortical processing of noxious and innocuous mechanical stimulation (Kenshalo et al., 2000; Lui et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Detailed fMRI analysis reveals a fine-grained somatotopy for nociceptive inputs in primary somatosensory (S1) cortex that are aligned with activation maps following innocuous tactile stimuli in adults.
source: detailed fMRI analysis reveals a fine-grained somatotopy for nociceptive inputs in primary somatosensory (S1) cortex that are aligned with activation maps following innocuous tactile stimuli, suggesting comparable cortical representations for mechanoreceptive and nociceptive signals (Mancini et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific fMRI study.

claim: A whole-body topographical map of innocuous mechanical stimulation develops in the sensorimotor cortices over the early postnatal period in rats.
source: A whole-body topographical map of innocuous mechanical stimulation develops in the sensorimotor cortices over the early postnatal period in rats, which represent the human final gestational trimester (Seelke et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study in rats.

claim: Distinct representations of the hands and feet can be observed from 31 weeks using fMRI.
source: Distinct representations of the hands and feet can be observed from 31 weeks using fMRI (Dall'Orso et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous fMRI study.

claim: Somatosensory representations become increasingly localised by term age.
source: becoming increasingly localised by term age (Allievi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Haemodynamic responses to a clinically required heel lance have been recorded from 28 weeks using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS).
source: While haemodynamic responses to a clinically required heel lance have been recorded from 28 weeks using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) (Slater et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous fNIRS study.

claim: Noxious and innocuous stimuli can be distinguished in EEG recordings from 34 to 35 weeks.
source: and can be distinguished from innocuous tactile evoked brain activity in EEG recordings from 34 to 35 weeks (Fabrizi et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous EEG study.

claim: The source of nociceptive activity and topographic representation of noxious and innocuous modalities have not been mapped, or their alignment established, in the infant cortex.
source: the source of this activity and topographic representation of these two modalities have not been mapped, or their alignment established, in the infant cortex.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Infant pain behaviour is exaggerated and disorganised in newborn rodents and human infants.
source: Infant pain behaviour is exaggerated and disorganised in newborn rodents and human infants (Fitzgerald, 2005; Fitzgerald, 2015; Cornelissen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on infant pain behavior.

claim: Poor spatial tuning of nociceptive reflexes and receptive fields is a feature of the developing somatosensory system.
source: Poor spatial tuning of nociceptive reflexes and receptive fields is a feature of the developing somatosensory system, followed by the emergence of adult organisation through activity-dependent refinement of synaptic connections (Beggs et al., 2002; Schouenborg, 2008; Koch and Fitzgerald, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on developmental neuroscience.

claim: The developmental process of synaptic refinement is reflected in ascending nociceptive signals to S1, leading to widespread S1 activation and poor spatial localisation of noxious events in early life.
source: We hypothesised that this developmental process is reflected in ascending nociceptive signals to S1, leading to widespread S1 activation and poor spatial localisation of noxious events in early life.
evidence: This is the hypothesis of the study, based on inference from developmental principles.

claim: Touch stimulation of the hand elicited significant increases in seven channels, with a maximum change (0.33 μM at 9.2 s post-stimulus) at the channel corresponding to the FCC5 position.
source: Touch stimulation of the hand elicited significant increases in seven channels, with a maximum change (0.33 μM at 9.2 s post-stimulus) at the channel corresponding to the FCC5 position of the 10:5 placement system (Oostenveld and Praamstra, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Touch of the heel elicited significant increases in seven channels, with a maximum change (0.35 μM at 15.8 s) at the channel corresponding to the CPP1 10:5 position.
source: while touch of the heel elicited significant increases in seven channels, with a maximum change (0.35 μM at 15.8 s) at the channel corresponding to the CPP1 10:5 position.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Hand touch elicited significant decreases in Δ[Hb] in eight channels with peak change of –0.18 μM at 17.6 s.
source: hand: significant decreases in eight channels [peak change: –0.18 μM at 17.6 s]
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Heel touch elicited significant decreases in Δ[Hb] in 14 channels with peak change of –0.21 μM at 11.1 s.
source: heel: significant decreases in 14 channels [peak change: –0.21 μM at 11.1 s]
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The topography of touch peak activation in the newborn infant S1 is consistent with the known adult S1 topography.
source: Image reconstruction of the channel data (Figure 2a and b) shows that the topography of touch peak activation in the newborn infant S1 is consistent with the known adult S1 topography: the area representing the foot lies in the superomedial postcentral gyrus, while the area for the hand is more lateral and inferior (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Harding-Forrester and Feldman, 2018; Willoughby et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to adult somatotopy studies.

claim: The area representing the foot lies in the superomedial postcentral gyrus in newborn infants.
source: the area representing the foot lies in the superomedial postcentral gyrus
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and comparison with adult anatomy.

claim: The area for the hand is more lateral and inferior in newborn infant S1.
source: while the area for the hand is more lateral and inferior (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Harding-Forrester and Feldman, 2018; Willoughby et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to adult somatotopy studies.

claim: Heel lance elicited significant increases in Δ[HbO] in eight channels, with a maximum increase (0.96 μM at 14.5 s) at the channel corresponding to the CP3h 10:5 position.
source: Heel lance elicited significant increases in Δ[HbO] in eight channels, with a maximum increase (0.96 μM at 14.5 s) at the channel corresponding to the CP3h 10:5 position.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Four of the channels with a significant increase in Δ[HbO] following the lance also had a significant increase in Δ[HbO] following touch of the heel.
source: Four of the channels with a significant increase in Δ[HbO] following the lance also had a significant increase in Δ[HbO] following touch of the heel.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from Figures 1b and 1c.

claim: Two channels displayed a significant increase following lance and also following touch of the hand, demonstrating a topographic overlap with both the hand and heel touch responses.
source: Notably two channels also displayed a significant increase following touch of the hand, demonstrating a topographic overlap with both the hand and heel touch responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c.

claim: Heel lance elicited significant decreases in Δ[Hb] in 11 channels with peak change of 1.03 μM at 9.1 s.
source: The accompanying decrease in concentration of deoxygenated haemoglobin (Δ[Hb]) was widespread (significant decreases in 11 channels; peak change 1.03 μM at 9.1 s)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Heel touch and lance elicited a peak increase in Δ[HbO] at the same latency and location.
source: Heel touch and lance elicited a peak increase in Δ[HbO] at the same latency and location (distance between peaks = 1.65 mm, p = 0.156; difference in peak latency = 2 s [14 vs. 16 s], p = 0.358; Figure 3a–b)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The peak Δ[HbO] response to heel lance was significantly larger than to heel touch (maximum Δ[HbO]: 16.06 vs. 5.43 μM, p = 0.001).
source: however this was significantly larger (maximum Δ[HbO]: 16.06 vs. 5.43 μM, p = 0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The peak Δ[HbO] response to heel lance was significantly wider than to heel touch (FWHM area: 51.41 vs. 43.79 mm2, p = 0.019).
source: and wider (FWHM area: 51.41 vs. 43.79 mm2, p = 0.019) following lance stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The overall area of activation was significantly more widespread following heel lance compared to heel touch (Δ[HbO] overall area: 455.27 vs. 259.51 mm², p = 0.009).
source: The overall area of activation was also significantly more widespread following heel lance (Δ[HbO] overall area: 455.27 vs. 259.51 mm², p = 0.009)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increase in Δ[HbO] was significantly larger following lance compared to touch across 50% of the lance-only activation area.
source: The increase in Δ[HbO] was significantly larger following lance compared to touch across 50% of the lance-only activation area (Figure 3a – red area, Figure 3c)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increase in Δ[HbO] was significantly larger following lance compared to touch across 26% of the overlap area.
source: and across 26% of the overlap area (Figure 3a – orange area, Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was no significant difference in Δ[HbO] changes between lance and touch across the touch-only activation area.
source: However, there was no significant difference in Δ[HbO] changes between lance and touch across the touch-only activation area (Figure 3a – pink area).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The significantly larger and wider peak response and more widespread overall area of activation following lance is not due to a greater systemic haemodynamic change following this stimulus.
source: This shows that the significantly larger and wider peak response and more widespread overall area of activation following lance is not due to a greater systemic haemodynamic change following this stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis showing regional differences rather than global changes.

claim: The location of the peak change in Δ[Hb] was significantly different following heel touch and lance (distance between peaks = 51.88 mm, p = 0.041).
source: The location, but not latency, of the peak change in Δ[Hb] was significantly different following heel touch and lance (distance between peaks = 51.88 mm, p = 0.041; difference in peak latency = –19.3 s [9.5 vs. 28 s], p = 0.028)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The peak Δ[Hb] response to heel lance was significantly larger than to heel touch (maximum Δ[Hb]: –22.54 to –6.62 μM, p < 0.001).
source: which was also significantly larger (maximum Δ[Hb]: –22.54 to –6.62 μM, p < 0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The peak Δ[Hb] response to heel lance was significantly wider than to heel touch (Δ [Hb] FWHM area: 15.31 vs. 4.63 mm2, p < 0.001).
source: and wider (Δ [Hb] FWHM area: 15.31 vs. 4.63 mm2, p < 0.001) following heel lance
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overall area of Δ[Hb] activation was significantly more widespread following heel lance compared to heel touch (Δ[Hb] overall area: 475.24 vs. 95.53 mm², p < 0.001).
source: The overall area of activation was also significantly more widespread following heel lance (Δ[Hb] overall area: 475.24 vs. 95.53 mm², p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The heel touch Δ[HbO] response is limited to the areas of the S1/M1 associated with the foot.
source: The key difference between the two patterns of activation is that the heel touch Δ[HbO] response is limited to the areas of the S1/M1 associated with the foot
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: The lance Δ[HbO] response extends towards other more ventral regions of S1.
source: whereas the lance Δ[HbO] response extends towards other more ventral regions of S1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: The adult primate S1 has a defined somatotopic organisation of tactile and nociceptive cortical receptive fields.
source: The adult primate S1 has a defined somatotopic organisation of tactile and nociceptive cortical receptive fields (Andersson et al., 1997; Kenshalo et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Adult S1 has spatially precise cortical maps of Aδ and Aβ afferent fibre input.
source: including spatially precise cortical maps of Aδ and Aβ afferent fibre input (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous research study.

claim: Human fMRI studies show that adult somatotopic maps of noxious and non-noxious mechanical stimulation substantially overlap.
source: Human fMRI studies show that adult somatotopic maps of noxious and non-noxious mechanical stimulation substantially overlap (Lui et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous fMRI study.

claim: Detailed analysis reveals a fine-grained somatotopy for nociceptive inputs in adult S1 cortex that are highly aligned with maps of innocuous tactile stimuli.
source: and detailed analysis reveals a fine-grained somatotopy for nociceptive inputs in S1 cortex that are highly aligned with maps of innocuous tactile stimuli, suggesting comparable cortical representations for mechanoreceptive and nociceptive signals (Mancini et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous research study.

claim: Comparable representation of mechanoreceptive and nociceptive signals is not present in the newborn infant S1 cortex.
source: Here, we have shown that this comparable representation is not present in the newborn infant S1 cortex.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Noxious mechanical stimulation evokes a larger peak increase in concentration of oxygenated haemoglobin (Δ[HbO]) compared to innocuous stimulation of the same body area.
source: Noxious mechanical stimulation evokes a larger peak increase in concentration of oxygenated haemoglobin (Δ[HbO]) and decrease in concentration of deoxygenated haemoglobin (Δ[Hb]) compared to innocuous stimulation of the same body area at comparable location and latency as reported elsewhere (Bartocci et al., 2006; Slater et al., 2006; Verriotis et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and citations to previous studies.

claim: Noxious mechanical stimulation evokes a larger peak decrease in concentration of deoxygenated haemoglobin (Δ[Hb]) compared to innocuous stimulation of the same body area.
source: Noxious mechanical stimulation evokes a larger peak increase in concentration of oxygenated haemoglobin (Δ[HbO]) and decrease in concentration of deoxygenated haemoglobin (Δ[Hb]) compared to innocuous stimulation of the same body area at comparable location and latency as reported elsewhere (Bartocci et al., 2006; Slater et al., 2006; Verriotis et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and citations to previous studies.

claim: The noxious activation is greater than the touch evoked activity presumably due to hyperaemia associated with greater depolarisation and spike activity within the activated areas.
source: The fact that the noxious activation is greater than the touch evoked activity is presumably due to hyperaemia associated with greater depolarisation and spike activity within the activated areas.
evidence: This is an inference based on known physiological mechanisms.

claim: The response to the lance is only significantly larger than touch in 50% of lance-only area of activation, 26% of the lance and touch overlap area, and nowhere in the touch-only activation area.
source: Although a lance, being a more intense stimulus, could be thought to cause more widespread cortical activation throughout the cortex, here the response to the lance is only significantly larger than touch in 50% of lance-only area of activation, 26% of the lance and touch overlap area, and nowhere in the touch-only activation area.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The response to a noxious and innocuous mechanical stimulus is not spatially aligned in newborn infants.
source: Our results instead suggest that the response to a noxious and innocuous mechanical stimulus is not spatially aligned.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The infant has a distinct somatotopic map for touch, similar to that described in adults.
source: Within S1 itself, the infant has a distinct somatotopic map for touch, similar to that described in adults, with the area representing the foot lying in the superomedial postcentral gyrus, and the area for the hand located more inferiorly (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Blake et al., 2002; Akselrod et al., 2017), consistent with previous reports in newborn infants (Dall'Orso et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and citations to previous studies.

claim: Noxious heel lance evokes widespread activity within S1, peaking in a similar area of the superomedial postcentral gyrus as touch activity, but extending to the hand representation area.
source: Noxious heel lance, on the other hand, evokes widespread activity within S1, peaking in a similar area of the superomedial postcentral gyrus as touch activity, but extending to the hand representation area.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: The S1 somatotopic nociceptive map is not as precise as the touch map in the newborn.
source: nevertheless, our data shows that the S1 somatotopic nociceptive map is not as precise as the touch map in the newborn.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: fNIRS is an indirect measure of neuronal activation and may be confounded by systemic vascular changes such as increases in blood pressure.
source: It should be noted that fNIRS is an indirect measure of neuronal activation and may be confounded by systemic vascular changes such as increases in blood pressure, which may be more likely following a noxious vs. innocuous stimulus.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on knowledge of fNIRS limitations.

claim: Global changes common across channels were removed using principal component analysis (PCA).
source: However, we removed global changes common across channels using principal component analysis (PCA)
evidence: This describes a methodological step in the data analysis.

claim: The greater magnitude of the heel lance response is not due to systemic changes elicited by the noxious stimulus.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the greater magnitude of the heel lance response is not due to systemic changes elicited by the noxious stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis showing regional rather than global differences.

claim: fNIRS is ideally suited to measuring cortical haemodynamic response to innocuous and noxious mechanical stimulation in neonates as recording can be performed at the infant cotside.
source: Measuring the cortical haemodynamic response to innocuous and noxious mechanical stimulation in neonates fNIRS is ideally suited to a study of this kind as recording and sensory stimulation, including clinically required heel lance, can be performed at the infant cotside (Bartocci et al., 2006; Slater et al., 2010; Kashou et al., 2017; Verriotis et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Other methods of measuring cortical response either do not provide sufficient spatial information and source localisation, such as EEG, or are limited by the use of experimental 'pinprick' stimulators that are not actually painful, such as in fMRI studies.
source: Other methods of measuring this either do not provide sufficient spatial information and source localisation, such as EEG recording of nociceptive-related ERPs (Fabrizi et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2018) or are limited by the use of experimental 'pinprick' stimulators, that for ethical reasons are not actually painful, such as in fMRI studies (Goksan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological comparison supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Simultaneous vertex EEG and fNIRS recordings over S1 show that haemodynamic and neural responses are related in magnitude.
source: The change in the Δ[HbO] and Δ[Hb] following sensory stimulation is an indirect measure of neural activity: simultaneous vertex EEG and fNIRS recordings over S1 show that haemodynamic and neural responses are related in magnitude (Verriotis et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Following all stimuli, channels showing a significant increase in Δ[HbO] also had a smaller decrease in Δ[Hb], consistent with the mature canonical response.
source: Following all stimuli, and consistent with the mature canonical response, channels showing a significant increase in Δ[HbO] also had a smaller decrease in Δ[Hb].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Regional overperfusion following neuronal activation, beyond that required by metabolic demands, means that less Hb is removed from the region compared to the oversupply of HbO.
source: Regional overperfusion following neuronal activation, beyond that required by metabolic demands, means that less Hb is removed from the region compared to the oversupply of HbO.
evidence: This is an explanation based on established physiological knowledge.

claim: The decrease in Δ[Hb] was more widespread (but smaller in magnitude) compared to the localised increase in Δ[HbO].
source: However, the decrease in Δ[Hb] was more widespread (but smaller in magnitude) compared to the localised increase in Δ[HbO].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: This type of response suggests that more blood is leaving the region (removing Hb) compared to the incoming supply (no significant change in Δ[HbO] in peripheral channels) due to immature regulation of cerebral blood flow (CBF).
source: This type of response, not previously reported in infants (de Roever et al., 2018), suggests that more blood is leaving the region (removing Hb) compared to the incoming supply (no significant change in Δ[HbO] in peripheral channels) due to immature regulation of cerebral blood flow (CBF).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and knowledge of developmental physiology.

claim: There are multiple mechanisms by which blood vessels dilate and CBF increases following neural activation, including arterial CO2 and O2 concentrations and astrocyte and pericyte activity.
source: There are multiple mechanisms by which blood vessels dilate and CBF increases following neural activation, including arterial CO2 and O2 concentrations, which relax/contract the smooth muscle cells of cerebral arteries and arterioles (Kety and Schmidt, 1948), and astrocyte and pericyte activity which controls vessel diameter and the propagation of vasodilation along the vascular tree (Takano et al., 2006; Cai et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on cerebrovascular physiology.

claim: Many mechanisms controlling cerebral blood flow are still developing in the newborn.
source: many of which are still developing in the newborn (Pryds and Greisen, 1989; Binmöller and Müller, 1992; Fujimoto, 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on developmental physiology.

claim: Rapid changes in CBF occur over the first postnatal days as cerebral circulation adapts.
source: leading to rapid changes in CBF over the first postnatal days as cerebral circulation adapts (Meek et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous research study.

claim: The infants in this study were held skin to skin, swaddled in their mother's arms in a naturalistic setting.
source: The infants in this study were held skin to skin, swaddled in their mother's arms in a naturalistic setting, which is a major advantage of fNIRS recording over fMRI for human developmental studies of brain function.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions of the study.

claim: Comparison of the time-series following heel touch with and without removing trials with known movement showed no significant difference.
source: Indeed, comparison of the time-series following heel touch with and without removing trials with known movement showed no significant difference (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 33–50% of babies grimaced for up to 7 s following the lance.
source: Furthermore, 33–50% of babies did grimace for up to 7 s following the lance
evidence: This is an observation from video recordings of the infants.

claim: If facial movements mediated the response following the lance, this would have prolonged the peak or duration of the change in [HbO], while in fact the latency and time course of the response to both stimuli was the same.
source: but if these facial movements mediated the response following the lance, this would have prolonged the peak or duration of the change in [HbO], while in fact the latency and time course of the response to both stimuli was the same (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data to rule out confounding effects.

claim: In humans, distinct representations of the hands and feet can be observed from 31 weeks' gestation, using fMRI.
source: In humans, distinct representations of the hands and feet can be observed from 31 weeks' gestation, using fMRI (Dall'Orso et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous fMRI study.

claim: Distinct representations of the hands and feet can be observed from 28 weeks using neural activity recorded from the scalp.
source: and from 28 weeks using neural activity recorded from the scalp (Donadio et al., 2018; Whitehead et al., 2018; Whitehead et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies using scalp recordings.

claim: The response to innocuous mechanical stimulation was more localised in S1 than the wider and less refined topographical map of noxious mechanical stimulation.
source: The response to innocuous mechanical stimulation was more localised in S1 than the wider and less refined topographical map of noxious mechanical stimulation
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The more localised innocuous response suggests a slower maturation of the S1 circuitry involved in nociceptive processing compared to touch processing in the infant brain.
source: suggesting a slower maturation of the S1 circuitry involved in nociceptive processing compared to touch processing in the infant brain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In rodents, at every level of the developing somatosensory central nervous system, tactile processing matures before nociceptive processing.
source: In rodents, at every level of the developing somatosensory central nervous system, tactile processing matures before nociceptive processing (Fitzgerald, 2005; Koch and Fitzgerald, 2013; Chang et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2020; Verriotis et al., 2016a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies in rodents.

claim: Widespread nociceptive cortical maps are consistent with infant pain behaviour, characterised by exaggerated and disorganised nociceptive reflexes in both rodent pups and human neonates.
source: Widespread nociceptive cortical maps are consistent with infant pain behaviour, characterised by exaggerated and disorganised nociceptive reflexes in both rodent pups and human neonates (Fitzgerald, 2005; Fitzgerald, 2015)
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to known behavioral observations, supported by citations.

claim: Infant nociceptive reflexes can fail to remove a body part from the source of pain.
source: and which can fail to remove a body part from the source of pain (Waldenström et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous research study.

claim: Nociceptive reflexes following noxious heel lance are larger in magnitude and significantly more prolonged in human infants compared to adults.
source: Nociceptive reflexes following noxious heel lance are larger in magnitude and significantly more prolonged in human infants compared to adults (Cornelissen et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous research study.

claim: Infant nociceptive reflexes have widespread cutaneous receptive fields that encompass the whole lower limb.
source: and have widespread cutaneous receptive fields that encompass the whole lower limb (Andrews and Fitzgerald, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous research study.

claim: This lack of organisation could be reflected in the ascending spinothalamic and thalamocortical projections, delaying the maturation of S1 cortical nociceptive maps in the newborn.
source: This lack of organisation could be reflected in the ascending spinothalamic and thalamocortical projections, delaying the maturation of S1 cortical nociceptive maps in the newborn.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the neural mechanisms underlying the observed findings.

claim: Initially, somatosensory maps are diffuse and overlapping, but in the rodent somatosensory cortex, excitatory thalamocortical afferents undergo activity-dependent refinement to sharpen these maps.
source: Initially, somatosensory maps are diffuse and overlapping, but in the rodent somatosensory cortex, excitatory thalamocortical afferents undergo activity-dependent refinement to sharpen these maps (Iwasato et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous research study in rodents.

claim: Inhibitory interneuron sensory maps expand over development in an experience-dependent manner.
source: Equally important is the maturation of inhibitory interneuron sensory maps which, in contrast, expand over development in an experience-dependent manner (Quast et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous research study.

claim: Slow developmental broadening of an inhibitory nociceptive network may explain the widespread nociceptive map in S1 and also the greater amplitude of EEG noxious responses in infants compared to adults.
source: Slow developmental broadening of an inhibitory nociceptive network may explain the widespread nociceptive map in S1 and also the greater amplitude of EEG noxious responses in infants compared to adults (Fabrizi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings, supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The widespread S1 nociceptive topography implies that the infant S1 cortex would be unable to accurately localise noxious events.
source: The widespread S1 nociceptive topography discovered here implies that the infant S1 cortex would be unable to accurately localise noxious events
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The infant S1 cortex may lack the computational ability to reliably send noxious information to higher brain centres.
source: and may lack the computational ability to reliably send noxious information to higher brain centres (Thivierge and Marcus, 2007; Harding-Forrester and Feldman, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings, supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Heel lance is one of many skin-breaking procedures commonly performed in neonatal hospital care.
source: Heel lance is one of many skin-breaking procedures commonly performed in neonatal hospital care (Laudiano-Dray et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study on neonatal care practices.

claim: Innocuous mechanical stimulation, such as touch, activates a spatially restricted and somatotopically defined cortical area.
source: This contrasts with innocuous mechanical stimulation, such as touch, which activates a spatially restricted and somatotopically defined cortical area.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Repeated noxious experiences have adverse effects upon the developing brain.
source: Increasing evidence that repeated noxious experiences have adverse effects upon the developing brain (Ranger and Grunau, 2014; Duerden et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Thirty-two infants (35–42 gestational weeks at birth, 0–7 days of age, 12 female) were recruited from the postnatal, special care, and high dependency wards within the neonatal unit at University College London Hospital.
source: Thirty-two infants (35–42 gestational weeks at birth, 0–7 days of age, 12 female; Table 1) were recruited from the postnatal, special care, and high dependency wards within the neonatal unit at University College London Hospital.
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: Six infants received touch stimulation of both the heel and hand.
source: Six infants received touch stimulation of both the heel and hand.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: This sample size is sufficient as similar high impact works using single trial noxious stimulation or multiple mechanical stimulations have yielded significant results with group sample sizes of 5–15 and 10–15.
source: This sample size is sufficient as similar high impact works using single trial noxious stimulation or multiple mechanical stimulations have yielded significant results with group sample sizes of 5–15 (Bartocci et al., 2006) and 10–15 (Arichi et al., 2012), respectively.
evidence: This justifies the sample size based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Infants wore a 21-channel array consisting of eight sources and eight detectors with inter-optode distances of 2.5–4 cm.
source: Infants wore a 21-channel array consisting of eight sources and eight detectors with inter-optode distances of 2.5–4 cm.
evidence: This describes the fNIRS recording setup.

claim: The array was secured over the pericentral area of the scalp on the side contralateral to the stimulation with a custom-designed textile cap.
source: The array was secured over the pericentral area of the scalp on the side contralateral to the stimulation with a custom-designed textile cap (EasyCap, Figure 4a).
evidence: This describes the fNIRS recording setup.

claim: This optode arrangement provided sensitivity coverage for the somatomotor cortex contralateral to the stimulation site and of the medial part on the ipsilateral side.
source: This optode arrangement provided sensitivity coverage for the somatomotor cortex contralateral to the stimulation site and of the medial part on the ipsilateral side (Figure 4d).
evidence: This describes the spatial coverage of the fNIRS recording.

claim: One source-detector pair was placed at a more ventral posterior location of the scalp (P7 of the international 10/5 positioning system) and worked as a control channel.
source: One source-detector pair was placed at a more ventral posterior location of the scalp (P7 of the international 10/5 positioning system) (Figure 4b). This channel was sensitive to the posterior temporal lobe and worked as a control channel (Figure 4b–d).
evidence: This describes the control channel in the experimental setup.

claim: A continuous wave recording system was used with two wavelengths of source light at 780 and 850 nm and a sampling rate of 10 Hz.
source: A continuous wave recording system was used with two wavelengths of source light at 780 and 850 nm and a sampling rate of 10 Hz to measure changes in oxy- and deoxy-haemoglobin concentration (Gowerlabs NTS fNIRS system).
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the fNIRS recording system.

claim: The noxious stimulus was a clinically required heel lance for blood sampling.
source: The noxious stimulus was a clinically required heel lance for blood sampling.
evidence: This describes the noxious stimulus used in the study.

claim: Blade release was time-locked to the NIRS recording using an accelerometer attached to the lancet.
source: Blade release was time-locked to the NIRS recording using an accelerometer attached to the lancet (Worley et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the synchronization method for the stimulus and recording.

claim: Innocuous mechanical stimulation was delivered by light touch on the lateral edge of the infants' palms and/or heels using a hand-held tendon hammer.
source: Innocuous mechanical stimulation was delivered by light touch on the lateral edge of the infants' palms and/or heels using a hand-held tendon hammer (ADInstruments).
evidence: This describes the innocuous stimulus used in the study.

claim: A train of up to 15 touches (average = 11.1) was delivered to each limb with a variable inter-stimulus interval of 35–60 s.
source: A train of up to 15 touches (average = 11.1) was delivered to each limb with a variable inter-stimulus interval of 35–60 s.
evidence: This describes the innocuous stimulation protocol.

claim: Stimulus repetition did not cause habituation of the response to touch.
source: Stimulus repetition did not cause habituation of the response to touch (no significant difference in the average time-series between the first and last 50% of the trials).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis showing no habituation effect.

claim: The four channels crossing over the midline had consistent poor signal quality (light intensity <0.01, SNR <2) and were not considered further.
source: The four channels crossing over the midline had consistent poor signal quality (light intensity <0.01, SNR <2) and were not considered further (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This describes data quality control and exclusion criteria.

claim: Recordings from 1 to 8 (average: 0.74) channels in 11 (29%) trials were removed for lance and touch stimuli.
source: Recordings from 1 to 8 (average: 0.74) channels in 11 (29%) trials were also removed for lance and touch stimuli.
evidence: This describes data quality control and exclusion.

claim: Motion artefacts were detected (change in amplitude >0.7 and/or change in standard deviation >15 over a 1 s time period) and then corrected using wavelet filtering.
source: Data were then converted into optical density, motion artefacts were detected (change in amplitude >0.7 and/or change in standard deviation >15 over a 1 s time period) and then corrected using wavelet filtering (Molavi and Dumont, 2012).
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing methods.

claim: Instrumental drift and cardiac artefact were removed with a 0.01–0.5 Hz bandpass filter.
source: Instrumental drift and cardiac artefact were removed with a 0.01–0.5 Hz bandpass filter.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing methods.

claim: Optical density changes recorded from all channels were removed using PCA; one component removed for every subject.
source: Optical density changes recorded from all channels (likely related to stimulus-dependent systemic physiological changes) were removed using PCA [Kozberg and Hillman, 2016; Tachtsidis and Scholkmann, 2016]; one component removed for every subject.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing methods.

claim: Data were converted into changes in oxy- and deoxy-haemoglobin concentration using the modified Beer–Lambert law with a differential path length factor of 4.39.
source: Finally, data were converted into changes in oxy- and deoxy-haemoglobin concentration (Δ[HbO] and Δ[Hb]) using the modified Beer–Lambert law (Delpy et al., 1988) with a differential path length factor of 4.39 (Wyatt et al., 1990).
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing methods.

claim: Despite the peak signal for lance being larger, the estimated SNR of the peak was lower, because more touch trials were averaged in this study.
source: Despite the peak signal for lance being larger, the estimated SNR of the peak was lower, because more touch trials were averaged in this study
evidence: This is an analysis of signal-to-noise ratio in the data.

claim: For each channel, significant changes in Δ[HbO] and Δ[Hb] were identified with a two-tailed t-test (α = 0.01) comparing each time point post-stimulus against the baseline.
source: For each channel, significant changes in Δ[HbO] and Δ[Hb] were identified with a two-tailed t-test (α = 0.01) comparing each time point post-stimulus against the baseline.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.

claim: Bonferroni correction was used for multiple comparisons (17 channels × 300 samples = 5100 comparisons).
source: Bonferroni correction was used for multiple comparisons (17 channels × 300 samples = 5100 comparisons).
evidence: This describes the statistical correction method.

claim: Only changes which were continuously significant for at least 1 s (10% of the length of the post-lance period) were retained.
source: Only changes (increases or decreases) which were continuously significant for at least 1 s (10% of the length of the post-lance period) were retained (Guthrie and Buchwald, 1991).
evidence: This describes the criteria for retaining significant changes.

claim: The fNIRS array was registered to a 39-week gestational age anatomical mesh model with 784,391 nodes.
source: The fNIRS array was registered to a 39-week gestational age anatomical mesh model with 784,391 nodes (Brigadoi et al., 2014) using tools from the AtlasViewer package (Aasted et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the image reconstruction method.

claim: Images were reconstructed using the DOT-HUB toolbox and the TOAST++ light transport modelling package, with zeroth-order Tikhonov regularisation with a regularisation hyperparameter of 0.1.
source: Images were reconstructed using the DOT-HUB toolbox (Cooper et al., 2021) and the TOAST++ light transport modelling package (Schweiger and Arridge, 2014a, Schweiger and Arridge, 2014b), with zeroth-order Tikhonov regularisation with a regularisation hyperparameter of 0.1.
evidence: This describes the image reconstruction method.
